subsystems.name: Command layer
subsystems.summary: internal/command is the write side of ZITADEL’s CQRS/event-sourcing core: nearly every state-changing gRPC/Connect call resolves to a Commands method covering users, orgs, instances, projects, IDPs, policies, providers, quotas, actions/executions, sessions, and groups. Errors cluster into three layers mapped to distinct gRPC codes: InvalidArgument for cheap syntactic validation before any eventstore read, NotFound/AlreadyExists for aggregate-existence checks against replayed write-model state, and PreconditionFailed for state-conditional rules discovered mid-command (not changed, already active, lockouts).

clusters.why: A shared low-level validation check failed somewhere in the request — a required field was left empty, malformed, or out of range. The exact wording is reused verbatim by dozens of unrelated checks across the command layer (most often identity-provider configuration fields, domain names, and settings values), so the field at fault depends on the specific error ID's call site, not the message text.

A required ID field on the request was left empty. The check is shared across dozens of unrelated resource types (schemas, SMTP/SMS configs, actions, applications, and more), so which ID is missing depends on the specific call site, not the message text.
The request omitted the organization ID (resourceOwner) that the target resource belongs to — every one of these commands needs an org ID to know which event stream to operate on.
The target user's ID was left empty on a user-scoped command such as deactivate, lock, reactivate, remove, or sign-out — ZITADEL needs a concrete user ID to know which account to act on.
The application payload failed basic validation — a required field like the app name is empty, or a type-specific requirement for the OIDC/SAML/API configuration wasn't met.
The submitted verification code — an init code, or a passwordless/passkey registration code — doesn't match what was generated and stored for this user, or it has expired.
The second-factor or multi-factor type passed when adding or removing a factor from a login policy isn't a recognized value — e.g. it was left unspecified.
A metadata key in the request is empty or otherwise fails validation when setting or bulk-removing metadata on a user or organization.
The SAML metadata XML — supplied directly or fetched from the metadata URL — couldn't be parsed as valid SAML metadata for the identity provider.
A metadata URL was given for a SAML identity provider, but fetching the XML from that URL failed, so no metadata was available to configure the provider despite the name.
An action-v2 execution condition must set exactly one of its mutually exclusive selectors (method/service/'all', or event/group/'all') — none, or more than one, was set.
The project ID, target user ID, or role list is missing, or one of the given roles isn't a valid project role, when adding, changing, or removing a project member.
The Apple identity provider's Services ID (client ID) field was left empty when adding or updating an Apple IDP configuration.
A verification code (phone, email, or OTP) was submitted as an empty string when trying to verify it.
The project ID, user ID, role list, or org/grant ID is missing when adding or changing a project grant member, or one of the given roles isn't a valid project-grant role.
A user grant ID — or one of the IDs in a bulk-remove list — was left empty when deactivating or removing a grant.
The private key bytes supplied for an Apple identity provider couldn't be parsed as a valid key — the content is malformed or corrupted.
The Apple identity provider's Key ID field, which identifies which private key signs the client secret, was left empty when adding or updating an Apple IDP configuration.
A password value was left empty when setting, changing, or checking a user's password — or, for a hash-based set, neither a plaintext password nor an encoded hash was given.
The Apple identity provider's Developer Team ID field was left empty when adding or updating an Apple IDP configuration.

Phone commands (add, verify, resend a code, remove) resolve the owning user first — the user's write model shows the account doesn't exist or was already removed, leaving no user to attach the phone number to.

The update request's values are identical to what's already stored, so there's nothing new to persist. This guard is shared by many 'change X' commands — OIDC/SAML app config, application name, OIDC settings — whenever the computed diff is empty.

An OTP check (TOTP, or OTP via SMS/email) was attempted before the user finished setting up that factor — its state isn't 'ready' yet, so there's no verified secret to check the submitted code against.
The identity provider ID referenced when starting a login/linking intent, or when adding an IDP link to a user, doesn't correspond to any IDP configured on the org or instance.
The user's account is currently locked — typically from too many failed verification attempts — so further recovery-code checks or removal are rejected until it's unlocked.

clusters.why: An internal session or MFA-setup helper needed the session's associated user ID, but it was empty — the session hasn't been linked to a user yet.

The target user is still in the 'initial' state — they haven't completed their invite/first-login flow — so actions that assume an active account, like requesting a password reset or verifying an email, are rejected until then.
A code check (email, phone, or OTP) was attempted before a code was ever requested for this user — no code is on record, or the configured code provider is missing.

During an OIDC token refresh, the presented refresh token doesn't match a currently active session, has passed its absolute or idle expiration, or doesn't parse into ZITADEL's expected <sessionID>:<tokenID> format.

A resend-code request — phone or email, on either the schema-user or human-user model — was made, but no code has ever been generated for this user; there's nothing to resend until an initial code is created.

Loading the org's domain/username policy (falling back to the instance default) failed while validating a username change or user removal — this wraps whatever underlying lookup error occurred, rather than pointing at one specific missing setting.
The user ID supplied — or auto-generated — when creating a human or machine user already belongs to an existing user account.
An internal WebAuthn/passkey helper — registering or verifying a credential, or sending a passwordless init code — needed the user ID, and sometimes a credential ID, but received an empty value.
The project grant's resource owner doesn't match the actual owning org of the project, or the grant is being created for the project's own organization — an org mismatch on the grant.

The project ID doesn't resolve to an active project for the given org. This is the same underlying condition as the NOT_FOUND variant, surfacing here because the project is checked as a precondition of another command rather than as its direct target.
A project role's resource owner doesn't match the resource owner of the project it's being added to or changed on — the role and its parent project disagree about which org owns them.
An OIDC access token being checked against a session doesn't match the session's current token, the session isn't active, or the token has already expired.

clusters.why: Generic internal-error fallback from the CockroachDB-backed static asset store (internal/static/database/crdb.go): building the SQL statement for an asset insert/select/delete failed, or the database round trip itself (query, scan, or exec) failed — for example because of a lost connection or constraint violation. The message carries no further detail beyond 'the asset store's database call failed.'

Defensive invariant check after an UPDATE scoped to a primary key in backend/v3 commands (session-factor checks, org activate/deactivate, …): the code expects exactly one row affected and throws this if more than one was. Since the WHERE clause always matches a primary key, this should be unreachable in normal operation — it guards against a data-integrity bug, not a condition an API caller can trigger.

Wraps read failures across the asset-storage backends: on the CockroachDB-backed store, a Scan against the assets table failed for a reason other than 'no rows' (e.g. a dropped connection); on the S3/minio-backed store, fetching an object's metadata or bytes failed at the storage API/network level. Affects reads of uploaded assets such as org logos, icons, or custom CSS.

Same failure class as Object could not be read but for deletes: the SQL DELETE against the assets table, or the S3/minio RemoveObject(s) call, failed at the database or storage-API level while removing one asset or all assets of a given type/instance.
